title: Knowledge Check 8: Lessons 57-64
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 57-64 of the agentic-ai series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Per the lesson, why does the per-invocation time budget fundamentally shape how you design a serverless agent?
options: It has no effect, because a single environment can be reused indefinitely across many invocations
It forces you to split fast answers from durable batch work, consuming one unit of durable work per invocation behind a queue rather than holding a long task open
It only applies to edge runtimes, never to Lambda or Cloud Run
It means every agent must run its whole loop inside a single invocation and cannot use a queue at all
questions.explanation: A serverless invocation has a hard time budget, so the durable worker pattern from Lesson 55 becomes the design driver: fast request-response work returns within the cap, while the batch backlog is consumed one unit of work per invocation behind a queue. Cold starts still happen on scale-up, but they delay one unit of work rather than a whole fleet.

questions.question: According to the lesson's description of Cloud Run autoscaling, what two metrics drive the number of instances, and what does that imply for an agent endpoint?
options: Queue depth and GPU utilization, so a background agent scales on its backlog
Memory utilization only, so a memory-heavy agent needs fewer instances to be profitable
Average CPU utilization and average request concurrency, so an interactive agent scales on the number of live callers it is currently serving
A fixed replica count set at deploy time, so autoscaling never changes the fleet
questions.explanation: Cloud Run's metrics-based scaling sizes instances from average CPU utilization and average request concurrency, clamped between minimum and maximum instance limits. For a user-facing agent, each chat or API call occupies one concurrent request, so the platform scales on the number of live callers rather than a backlog, which is the mirror image of queue-driven scaling.

questions.question: Why does the Vercel AI SDK earn a place in a serverless lesson rather than an earlier one, per the text?
options: It is the only hosting platform that can run a Lambda function
It replaces the model API entirely, so you no longer call a provider

Streaming is how a disposable, stateless serverless instance can feel like a live conversation, because tokens and tool messages flow back to the client as they are produced even though the instance may vanish as soon as the request ends
It is required before an agent may be deployed at the edge
questions.explanation: The AI SDK's streamText streams tokens and tool-call and tool-result messages back to the client as they are produced, so a serverless instance that is gone the moment the request finishes still delivers a clean, live-feeling response. The toolkit is the bridge between a stateless platform and an interface that appears continuous.

questions.question: Per the lesson, why does quantization usually come before any other decision when you are choosing a model for a local machine?
options: It has no real effect, because every model loads at its full precision no matter how it is stored
It only changes the training cost, not the memory needed to run the model
It stores weights in fewer bits, shrinking a model's memory footprint by about four times at 4-bit versus 16-bit, which is what decides whether the weights fit in VRAM or unified memory at all
It only applies to GGUF files and never to the engines that actually run the model
questions.explanation: Quantization stores each weight in fewer bits, so a 7B model drops from roughly 14 GB of fp16 weights to roughly 4 GB at 4-bit. That is the lever that lets a small GPU or a laptop hold a model that otherwise would never fit.

questions.question: Using the lesson's rule of thumb, about how much memory should an 11-billion-parameter model's weights need at 4-bit quantization?
options: About 2 GB, because parameter count is unrelated to memory
About 6.6 GB, from budgeting roughly 0.6 GB per billion parameters
About 22 GB, because each parameter always needs two bytes regardless of how it is stored
Exactly 11 GB, because one billion parameters equals one gigabyte
questions.explanation: The lesson's rule of thumb is roughly 0.6 GB of memory per billion parameters at 4-bit. For 11 billion parameters that is about 6.6 GB of weights, before adding context-window and runtime headroom.

questions.question: According to the lesson, what mainly sets the single-stream speed of a locally running model for one user?
options: How fast memory can move the model's weights into the compute units, roughly tokens per second equals memory bandwidth divided by bytes of model
The exact spelling of the prompt, because tokenization dominates all latency
The number of concurrent users, because one user always runs at the same speed no matter the hardware
The network round trip to the model provider, since local models still depend on a hosted API
questions.explanation: For one user, inference is bounded by how quickly the machine can stream weights from memory into the compute units. A smaller quantized model moves fewer bytes per token, which is why it feels faster on the same hardware.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Model Routing: Small Models, Cascades, and the Cost/Quality Balance", what is the key distinction between a router and a cascade?
options: A router calls models one after another while a cascade makes a single model choice up front
A router picks the model once before the call, while a cascade starts cheap and escalates only when the cheap answer fails a consistency or confidence check
A router is always a hand-written rule while a cascade is always a learned model
A router reduces latency while a cascade reduces cost
questions.explanation: The lesson states: routing picks the right model once before the call, while a cascade calls one model after another and escalates only when the cheap answer fails a consistency or confidence check.

questions.question: The lesson's worked example on a support-ticket triage agent keeps which category of traffic on the strong model by rule, regardless of difficulty?
options: Billing tickets, because they are the most frequent
Feature requests, because they drive product decisions
Security and compliance tickets, because routing is a cost lever and not a security boundary
All low-difficulty tickets, to keep routing decisions simple
questions.explanation: Step 3 says keep security and compliance tickets on the strong model by rule, and the pattern section repeats: never let a router guess on privileged or anti-fraud traffic.

questions.question: How does the lesson say a cascade decides whether to escalate a cheap model's answer to a stronger model?
options: By never escalating, since routing already handled the choice
By always escalating, because the cheap model is never trusted
By a static schedule that escalates every Nth request
By a verifier or discriminator that scores the answer, or by looking for disagreement among several cheap samples, escalating when the score is low or the answers diverge
questions.explanation: The lesson's cascade section says two mechanisms dominate: a verifier or discriminator scores the candidate and escalation triggers below a threshold, or the system asks several cheap models/samples and escalates when they disagree.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Caching Strategies: Semantic Caching, Response Caching, and Invalidation", which of the three LLM cache layers carries the highest risk of serving a wrong or mis-scoped answer?
options: Provider prefix caching, because it matches exactly and bills the repeated prefix at a discount
Exact-match response caching, because it hashes the whole request and only fires on identical input
Semantic caching, because it matches on embedding similarity by a threshold and can treat embedding-close as meaning-equal
None of the three layers carry any risk of a wrong answer
questions.explanation: The lesson orders the three layers by reach and risk and states that semantic caching is the only one that can confidently serve the wrong thing, because 'similar' is a judgment call made by a similarity threshold rather than an exact match. Prefix and exact-match caching match identical text or hashes and are described as safe.

questions.question: The lesson's worked example of a support assistant assigns which routing to each route?
options: Semantic caching for the personalized account-history route, exact-match for the product FAQ, and provider prefix caching for staging
Semantic caching for the low-risk product FAQ, a stricter scoped semantic cache for the conversational per-tenant support route, and exact-match caching for the staging environment
Provider prefix caching for every route, since it is the safest layer
Semantic caching for the staging environment and no caching at all for the FAQ
questions.explanation: The worked example puts the low-risk FAQ on semantic caching with a tolerant threshold, the conversational per-tenant support route on a stricter scoped semantic cache whose namespace includes the system-prompt version, and the staging environment on exact-match caching. The personalized account-history route gets no semantic cache.

questions.question: Why, per the lesson, must the system-prompt version be encoded into the cache namespace, and what does this have to do with invalidation?
options: Because system prompts never change, so the version is only needed for audit logging
Because encoding the version improves the embedding model's similarity scores
Because it is unnecessary; TTLs alone always expire stale entries in time
Because the system-prompt version rolls the cache forward when bumped, so improved prompts are not contradicted by stale cached answers from the old version until their TTL expires
questions.explanation: The lesson names version (via the namespace) as one of the two invalidation triggers: bumping the system-prompt version rolls the cache forward so old-configuration answers are never matched again. It calls the failure to invalidate on a prompt change a subtle, common bug where the prompt improves but cached answers keep reflecting the old one.

questions.question: A support agent must answer: 'Who approved the budget on this contract, and which of that person's direct reports changed the price?' Which memory backend is the right fit for this question, and why?
options: Vector memory, because it matches the query by meaning against past message chunks.
A knowledge graph, because the question follows explicit approval and reporting relationships that vector similarity alone cannot trace.
Neither; this is a prompt-engineering problem with no memory store involved.
A keyword index, because the question depends on exact string matches.
questions.explanation: The question is relational: it follows an approval chain and a reporting chain. The lesson notes that vector search reasons over semantic closeness rather than explicit relationships, while a knowledge graph represents entities as nodes and relationships as typed edges, so tracing the path from customer to contract to approver to direct reports is graph traversal work.

questions.question: A team is starting a research agent that must recall general topics a user discussed, tolerating paraphrased reminders. Per the lesson's recommended growth path, what should they build first?
options: A knowledge graph, so exact relationships are captured from the very first session.
A vector store, for fast fuzzy semantic recall, adding a knowledge graph later for high-value entities and core relationships as reasoning demands grow.
A relational SQL table of keyword tags for every conversation.
Only the context window, with no external memory store at all.
questions.explanation: The lesson calls vector memory the closest thing to a default, ideal for broad semantic recall and fuzzy matching with low setup cost. It then recommends starting agent memory with a vector store for conversational grounding and introducing a knowledge graph for high-value entities as reasoning requirements grow, rather than building a graph, which has a cold-start problem, up front.

questions.question: In the hybrid retrieval pattern the lesson recommends, what job does the vector search perform and what job does the graph traversal perform?
options: The vectors resolve the relational path and the graph performs the fuzzy similarity search.
The vectors find entry points and candidate entities, and traversal follows relationships outward from those points to pull precise relational context.
Both stores run identical queries on every turn and the results are averaged together.
The graph stores the embeddings and the vector store holds the edges.
questions.explanation: The lesson describes the hybrid as using vectors to find the entry points and candidate entities, then traversing the graph outward from those points to gather precise relational context. It calls this 'vectors for the entry point, graphs for the depth' and notes it is the pattern GraphRAG and Mem0 both follow.

questions.question: In the lesson's opening example, why did the LangChain team's demo report "4 open tickets" when a Cypher query found five?
options: The vector index was capped at four retrieved rows by design
Vector search retrieved the four most similar task chunks and the model assumed those four were the whole population, missing the rest
The query embedded the wrong text field fore quite query
The graph contained no task nodes, so the count was defaulted to four
questions.explanation: The opening says vector search retrieved the four most similar task chunks, and the LLM assumed those four were the whole population. Similarity returned text that sounds like the question, not a count of every open task.

questions.question: In the four-step knowledge graph retrieval loop from the Redis guide, what comes immediately after linking the query's entities to matching nodes in the graph?
options: Traverse the graph by generating a graph query, for example in Cypher, that walks the relationships the question needs
Re-embed the entire graph so the vector index reflects new connections
Run a whole-corpus aggregation over every node before answering
Drop any entity whose similarity score falls below the top-N threshold
questions.explanation: The loop is: extract entities, link query entities via vector search, traverse the graph with a generated graph query, then generate the response grounded in the retrieved graph context.

questions.question: Which three question shapes does the lesson say a knowledge graph genuinely beats vector memory on?
options: Relationship-path, multi-hop queries; whole-corpus aggregation questions; and dense, interconnected domains like dependency or citation graphs
Text-similarity lookups; full-text keyword searches; and linguistic paraphrase recall
Standalone fact questions; single-document summaries; and token-length optimization targets
Image retrieval; numeric range filters; and fuzzy date matching across logs
questions.explanation: The lesson lists three shapes where resemblance fails and the graph wins: relationship-path/multi-hop queries, whole-corpus questions like top-themes-in-tickets, and dense, interconnected domains where everything looks similar to everything else.

questions.question: In the lesson's worked example, why does the support triage router use a semantic label like support-triage-router-v1.1.0 instead of just saving a new file?
options: Semantic versioning makes the file name shorter and easier to type in the terminal
It records the change history and lets the team roll back and identify which version runs in which environment
It is the only format the open-source eval tool accepts for test cases
It forces a full application redeploy on every prompt edit, which is the intended safety mechanism
questions.explanation: The lesson says versioning applies code-style tracking to prompts: a history of what changed and why, ability to roll back, and a record of which version runs in which environment. A semantic label like support-triage-router-v1.1.0 is that identity. It is about history and environments, not about OS compatibility or the eval tool.

questions.question: In the lesson's prompt regression workflow, what does the test suite do that a code commit message cannot?
options: It rewrites the prompt in a syntax the model parses faster
It verifies the prompt text is grammatically correct before deploy
It pins the behavior the queue depends on and blocks a change below a pass-rate threshold, catching regressions before users hit them
It signs the prompt with a cryptographic hash so no one can edit it
questions.explanation: The lesson describes a regression suite that pins the behavior a system depends on, for example routing a billing question to billing and an outage report to urgent, and blocks the deploy when the pass rate falls. Version history records that something changed; the eval suite is the gate that catches whether a change broke behavior before it reaches users.

questions.question: In the lesson's prompt ops layer, why does the team attach the prompt version to every production call and pair traces with evaluations?
options: To prove the prompt passes a spell check before it is published to the library
To increase token usage so cost reporting shows higher utilization
To make it impossible for another team to copy the prompt
So a quality drop becomes attributable: a trace-linked evaluation jumps from a flagged response to the exact prompt version, context, and model parameters that caused it
questions.explanation: The lesson's core prompt-ops habit is pairing trace and evaluation. Aggregate scoring says a problem exists; trace-linked evaluation supplies the why, because a 200-status LLM response can still be wrong, and the trace shows whether the drop correlates with a prompt version, model route, or retrieval source.

questions.question: A company's agent answers plausibly but wrongly because the pricing catalog it needs changed last month, and it also writes replies in a flat voice it cannot seem to fix with better prompting. Applying the lesson's core distinction, which statement is correct?
options: Both gaps are behavior gaps, so fine-tuning alone is the right answer and retrieval adds nothing.
The stale-facts gap is a knowledge problem best handled by RAG because it can cite and stay current, while the flat-voice gap is a behavior problem that fine-tuning is suited to carry in weights.
Both gaps are knowledge gaps, so a single RAG pipeline fixes everything without any model training.
Neither approach can address both, so the system should avoid using its own data entirely.
questions.explanation: The lesson's core distinction is that RAG changes what the model sees and fine-tuning changes how it behaves. Missing or stale catalog facts are a knowledge gap that retrieval handles, because indexed today's or yesterday's data appears at inference time with no retraining. A flat, off-brand voice is a behavior gap that a fine-tuned model can carry reliably in its weights. The lesson emphasizes this is the one-line rule: fine-tuning adjusts behavior, style, and format, while retrieval is the tool for current facts.

questions.question: For a legal assistant whose statutes change several times a quarter, needs to cite the exact source document behind every answer, and must withhold certain cases from users without clearance, which choice does the lesson's framework favor first and why?
options: Fine-tuning, because baking the statutes into model weights makes answers faster with no retrieval infrastructure to maintain.
Fine-tuning, because a trained model can reliably reproduce legal terminology, which is more important than currency.
RAG, because the knowledge changes frequently, answers must be traceable to a source, and per-user access control is enforced by the retrieval layer.
RAG only if the company has many labeled question-answer pairs; the framework ranks that above freshness and citations.
questions.explanation: The framework's questions two and three push toward RAG. Knowledge that changes frequently favors retrieval because indexed updates appear with no retraining. RAG also supplies provenance, since the retrieved passage is passed explicitly and can be cited, and it honors per-user access because the retrieval layer can withhold segments a user is not permitted to see, something baked-in weights cannot do. Labeled pairs affect whether fine-tuning is feasible, but they do not outweigh the freshness, citation, and access-control requirements the scenario sets.

questions.question: A team fine-tunes a model on its invoice-processing workflow so the output format is always valid JSON, and separately builds a RAG layer that supplies the currently approved pricing and tax tables at inference time. Which statement best matches the lesson's guidance on this design?
options: This is the hybrid pattern the lesson recommends: fine-tune the durable behavior, retrieve the current facts, and the two together beat either approach alone for complex use cases.
This is wasteful because fine-tuning already carries the pricing data in its weights, so the RAG layer is redundant.
Fine-tuning and RAG should never be combined, since retrieval context overrides anything the model learned.
The RAG layer should be removed because an output-format model produces identical results whether or not it receives context.
questions.explanation: The repeated example in the lesson, the support agent, uses exactly this split, and the sourcing states it as the mature enterprise default: a fine-tuned model handles domain understanding and output format while RAG supplies the latest facts at inference time, and the combination outperforms either alone for complex use cases. The JSON formatting is a durable behavior for fine-tuning to own, while the pricing and tax tables are current facts that belong in the retrieval layer.
